rows.stem: A compound \(\mathrm{CaCl_2 \cdot 6H_2O}\) undergoes complete dissociation in water. The Van't Hoff factor 'i' is :
rows.solution:
The van't Hoff factor is 3.

Count the particles the formula unit actually releases into solution:
\(\mathrm{CaCl_2 \cdot 6H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ca^{2+}} + 2\mathrm{Cl^-} + 6\mathrm{H_2O}\)

That is ONE calcium ion and TWO chloride ions — three particles in all.

The six water molecules do NOT count. They are WATER OF CRYSTALLISATION, held in the solid lattice, and the moment the salt dissolves they simply become part of the SOLVENT. A colligative property counts solute particles against solvent molecules, so water added to the water cannot raise the count.

Including them would have given 9, which is the trap the formula is written to set. The hydrated and anhydrous salts give the SAME van't Hoff factor and the same freezing point depression for the same number of moles.

rows.stem: For a zero order reaction of the type \(\mathrm{A} \rightarrow\) products, the rate equation may be expressed as :
rows.solution:
The correct form is \(k = \dfrac{[\mathrm{A}]_0 - [\mathrm{A}]}{t}\).

A zero order reaction proceeds at a CONSTANT rate, independent of concentration:
\(\text{Rate} = -\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = k\)

Integrating between the start and time \(t\) gives the straight line
\([\mathrm{A}] = [\mathrm{A}]_0 - kt\)
which rearranges directly to the answer.

Two checks settle it without integrating. The rate constant must be POSITIVE, and the concentration FALLS, so the initial value must come first in the numerator — that rules out the second option. And the units must be those of a rate, concentration divided by time, which rules out the form with time in the numerator.

The factor of 2 in the third option has no origin in the derivation; it belongs to the HALF-LIFE expression, \(t_{1/2} = [\mathrm{A}]_0/2k\), which is a different quantity.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\) halide is not known ?
rows.solution:
COPPER(II) IODIDE is not known.

The other three copper(II) halides all exist — the fluoride, the chloride and the bromide. The iodide does not, because iodide is a REDUCING agent and copper(II) an oxidising one, so the two react instead of combining:
\(2\mathrm{Cu^{2+}} + 4\mathrm{I^-} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cu_2I_2} + \mathrm{I_2}\)

Copper is reduced to the \(+1\) state and iodide oxidised to iodine, so an attempt to prepare copper(II) iodide yields white copper(I) iodide and free iodine instead.

Two things make copper(I) the stable partner here. Iodide is the most easily oxidised of the halides, its electron being held least tightly; and copper(I) iodide is highly INSOLUBLE, so precipitating it drives the reaction forward.

This reaction is used analytically: the iodine liberated is titrated against thiosulphate to estimate copper.

The three compounds exhibit HYDRATE ISOMERISM.

They have the same overall composition but differ in how many WATER molecules are coordinated to the chromium and how many sit outside as water of CRYSTALLISATION — with the chlorides making up the difference in each case.

The consequences are visible and measurable. The three are different colours — violet, blue-green and dark green. And they give different amounts of precipitate with silver nitrate, since only the chloride OUTSIDE the sphere is free to react: the first gives three moles of silver chloride per mole, the second two, the third one.

That precipitate test is what identifies each compound, and it is the same reasoning Werner used to work out coordination numbers.

The other three options need something absent here: linkage isomerism needs an ambidentate ligand, geometrical isomerism needs a fixed spatial arrangement to differ, and ionization isomerism would need the exchanged groups to be something other than water.

rows.stem: Which of the following alkenes on acid catalysed hydration gives a tertiary alcohol ?
rows.solution:
2-METHYLPROPENE gives a tertiary alcohol.

Acid catalysed hydration goes through a CARBOCATION, so it follows MARKOVNIKOV'S RULE — the hydroxyl ends up on the carbon that can best support a positive charge, which is the more substituted one.

Protonating \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C{=}CH_2}\) at the terminal \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) leaves the positive charge on the carbon carrying two methyl groups, giving a TERTIARY cation, and water then attacks there:
\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C{=}CH_2} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{H^+}]{\mathrm{H_2O}} \mathrm{(CH_3)_3C{-}OH}\)

The product is 2-methylpropan-2-ol, a tertiary alcohol.

None of the others can give one. Propene and 1-butene are straight chain and give secondary alcohols, propan-2-ol and butan-2-ol; 2-butene likewise gives butan-2-ol. A tertiary alcohol needs a carbon bonded to three other carbons, and only the BRANCHED alkene here has one.

rows.stem: When nitrobenzene is heated with tin and concentrated HCl, the product formed is :
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — the four options are drawn benzene rings bearing, in order, —NH2, —NH3(+) Cl(-), —N=N—C6H5 and —Cl. They are named losslessly in the option text above, so the row is answerable from text, but the printed option block is worth attaching. Page idx 4, lower half.
rows.solution:
The product is ANILINE.

Tin with concentrated hydrochloric acid generates nascent hydrogen, which reduces the nitro group all the way to an amino group:
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NO_2} + 6[\mathrm{H}] \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Sn}/\mathrm{conc.\ HCl}} \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Six hydrogen atoms are needed, the nitrogen falling from \(+3\) to \(-3\).

In the acidic mixture the amine is of course present as its SALT, and the free amine is liberated by making the solution alkaline at the end — that step is part of the standard work-up, and the product isolated is aniline.

Azobenzene would require a CONTROLLED reduction in neutral or alkaline medium, which stops at an intermediate stage rather than going through to the amine. Chlorobenzene cannot form at all — nothing here replaces the nitro group by chlorine.

Corrosion of iron is an ELECTROCHEMICAL process.

It is not simply iron combining with oxygen. The rusting surface acts as a tiny GALVANIC CELL, with different patches of the same piece of metal serving as electrodes and a film of moisture carrying dissolved carbon dioxide or salt as the electrolyte.

At the ANODIC patches iron is oxidised:
\(\mathrm{Fe(s)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + 2e^-\), \(E^{\circ} = -0{\cdot}44\) V

At the CATHODIC patches oxygen from the air is reduced, taking up those electrons:
\(\mathrm{O_2} + 4\mathrm{H^+} + 4e^- \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2O}\), \(E^{\circ} = +1{\cdot}23\) V

The iron(II) ions are then oxidised further by air to hydrated iron(III) oxide, which is rust.

Two observations confirm the electrochemical picture: rusting stops in DRY air and in oxygen-free water, since a cell needs both an electrolyte and something to reduce; and it is FASTER in salt water, which conducts better. It is also why cathodic and sacrificial protection work at all.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: The number of molecules that react with each other in an elementary reaction is a measure of the :
rows.solution:
The number is a measure of the MOLECULARITY of the reaction.

Molecularity counts the species that must COLLIDE SIMULTANEOUSLY in a single elementary step — one for unimolecular, two for bimolecular, three for termolecular.

It is a THEORETICAL quantity, read off the mechanism, and it follows that it must be a whole number of at least 1 and cannot exceed about 3, three-body collisions being rare.

ORDER is the tempting alternative, and the distinction is the point of the question. Order is EXPERIMENTAL, read off the measured rate law, and it may be zero, fractional or negative. Order also applies to a complex reaction as a whole, while molecularity is defined only for a SINGLE elementary step.

The two coincide only for an elementary reaction, where the step IS the reaction — which is exactly the case the question specifies.

rows.stem: On hydrolysis, which of the following carbohydrates gives glucose and galactose ?
rows.solution:
LACTOSE gives glucose and galactose on hydrolysis.

Lactose is the sugar of MILK, a disaccharide built from one \(\beta\)-galactose unit and one glucose unit:
\(\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \text{glucose} + \text{galactose}\)

The others each give something else. SUCROSE gives glucose and FRUCTOSE; MALTOSE gives two molecules of glucose; CELLULOSE, a polymer of \(\beta\)-glucose, gives glucose alone.

Lactose is a REDUCING sugar, because the glucose unit keeps a free anomeric carbon and can still open into its aldehyde form — unlike sucrose, in which both anomeric carbons are locked into the linkage.

rows.stem: The deficiency of which of the following vitamins causes 'Rickets' ?
rows.solution:
Rickets is caused by a deficiency of VITAMIN D, calciferol.

Vitamin D controls the absorption of calcium and phosphate from the gut, so without it the growing bones fail to calcify properly. In children the soft bones bend under the body's weight, giving the characteristic bowed legs; the adult form of the same deficiency is called osteomalacia.

It is unusual among vitamins in being made by the body itself — the skin synthesises it from a cholesterol derivative on exposure to SUNLIGHT — so the deficiency appears where sunlight is scarce.

It is FAT SOLUBLE and therefore STORED in the liver, so it need not be supplied daily. The other options belong elsewhere: vitamin A gives night blindness, vitamin C scurvy, and the B group beri-beri and pernicious anaemia.

rows.subtopic: Chemical Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
rows.stem: Which of the following is an 'Acetal' ?

options.label: B
options.text: A five-membered ring drawn as \(\mathrm{(H_3C)_2C}\) bonded to two oxygen atoms, each oxygen in turn bonded to a \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) group, the two \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) groups being joined to each other

rows.solution:
The acetal is \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH(OCH_3)_2}\), 1,1-dimethoxyethane.

An ACETAL has ONE carbon bonded to TWO \(-\mathrm{OR}\) groups, and that carbon must also carry a HYDROGEN — it came from an aldehyde. Here the central carbon holds two methoxy groups, a methyl and a hydrogen, which fits exactly.

It is formed from an aldehyde and two molecules of alcohol under dry acid:
\(\mathrm{CH_3CHO} + 2\mathrm{CH_3OH} \xrightarrow{\text{dry HCl}} \mathrm{CH_3CH(OCH_3)_2} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

Test the others. \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2{-}OCH_3}\) is a plain ETHER, with only one oxygen. \(\mathrm{CH_3{-}CH(OH)(OCH_3)}\) has one \(-\mathrm{OH}\) and one \(-\mathrm{OR}\) on the same carbon, which makes it a HEMIACETAL — the intermediate stage, formed from one molecule of alcohol. The cyclic structure has two \(-\mathrm{OR}\) groups on one carbon but that carbon carries two METHYL groups and no hydrogen, so it came from a KETONE and is a ketal.

Acetal formation is reversible, which is why it is used to PROTECT a carbonyl group: the acetal survives base and hydride, and dilute acid gives the aldehyde back.

rows.stem: The crystal field splitting energy in tetrahedral crystal field \((\Delta_{\mathrm{t}})\) is equal to :
rows.solution:
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{t}} = \dfrac{4}{9}\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\).

Two things make the tetrahedral splitting the smaller. There are only FOUR ligands rather than six, so less charge surrounds the metal; and none of them points DIRECTLY at a d orbital, the ligands approaching between the axes rather than along them, so the interaction is weaker still.

The two effects together give roughly four-ninths, for the same metal and the same ligands at the same distance.

The consequence is decisive and worth remembering. That figure is essentially always SMALLER than the pairing energy, so electrons prefer to occupy the upper orbitals singly rather than pair up — tetrahedral complexes are therefore HIGH SPIN, and low spin ones are practically unknown.

The splitting is also INVERTED relative to the octahedral case: the \(e\) set lies lower and the \(t_2\) set higher, the reverse of the octahedral order.

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : When NaCl is added to water, a depression in freezing point is observed.
Reason (R) : The vapour pressure of solution is increased which causes depression in freezing point.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Adding sodium chloride to water does depress the freezing point, and sharply, since each formula unit gives two ions.

But the Reason has the direction of the vapour pressure wrong. Adding a non-volatile solute LOWERS the vapour pressure of the solution, it does not increase it — solute particles occupy part of the surface, so fewer solvent molecules escape from it.

And that LOWERING is exactly what causes the depression. A liquid freezes where its vapour pressure equals that of the solid; lowering the liquid's curve moves that meeting point to a LOWER temperature.

So the Reason names the right mechanism with the wrong sign. Had the vapour pressure genuinely risen, the freezing point would have been ELEVATED, and the Assertion would then have been false.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Limiting molar conductivity \((\Lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{m}})\) is obtained by the extrapolation of the \(\Lambda_{\mathrm{m}}\) versus \(\mathrm{C}^{1/2}\) curve of strong electrolyte.
Reason (R) : \(\Lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{m}}\) for weak electrolytes is obtained by using Kohlrausch's law.
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true, but the Reason is NOT the correct explanation of the Assertion.

The Assertion is correct. For a STRONG electrolyte the plot of \(\Lambda_m\) against \(\sqrt{\mathrm{C}}\) is a straight line over a useful range, because full dissociation means the only thing changing with dilution is how much the ions interfere with one another. Extrapolating that line to zero concentration gives \(\Lambda_m^{\circ}\) directly.

The Reason is also correct. For a WEAK electrolyte the curve rises steeply near infinite dilution and never meets the axis, so there is no intercept to extrapolate to, and Kohlrausch's law must be used instead — adding the limiting molar conductivities of the individual ions.

But the two statements describe DIFFERENT cases. The Reason concerns weak electrolytes while the Assertion concerns strong ones, so it cannot explain it; it supplies the CONTRASTING case, which is a different thing. Both are true, and each is worth knowing, but they stand side by side rather than one resting on the other.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(\mathrm{E}^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}/\mathrm{Cu}}\) is positive \((+\,0{\cdot}34\ \mathrm{V})\).
Reason (R) : Copper has high \(\Delta_{\mathrm{a}}\mathrm{H}^{\circ}\) and low \(\Delta_{\mathrm{hyd}}\mathrm{H}^{\circ}\).
rows.context: For Questions number 15 to 18, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (a), (b), (c) and (d) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Both statements are true and the Reason IS the correct explanation of the Assertion.

Copper is the ONLY metal in the 3d series with a positive standard reduction potential, which is why it does not dissolve in hydrochloric or dilute sulphuric acid — it cannot displace hydrogen.

The Reason explains it correctly. Converting solid copper into hydrated copper(II) ions takes three steps, and the energy released in the last must pay for the first two:
ATOMISATION — copper's \(\Delta_a\mathrm{H}^{\circ}\) is HIGH, so pulling an atom out of the metal costs a great deal.
IONISATION — removing two electrons costs more.
HYDRATION — the energy recovered when the ion is surrounded by water, and copper's \(\Delta_{\text{hyd}}\mathrm{H}^{\circ}\) is NOT high enough to cover the earlier costs.

The books do not balance, so the overall process is unfavourable, the equilibrium lies on the side of the METAL, and the reduction potential comes out positive at \(+0{\cdot}34\) V.

The practical consequence is copper's use for pipes, wiring and coinage: it is not attacked by water or by non-oxidising acids. Nitric acid does dissolve it, but by oxidising it rather than by displacing hydrogen.

rows.stem:
Write IUPAC names of the following :
(a) \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2(H_2O)(CN)]^{2+}}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{[Ni(NH_3)_6]Cl_2}\)
rows.solution:
(a) Fix the oxidation state first. Ethane-1,2-diamine and water are NEUTRAL, the cyanido ligand gives \(-1\), and the ion carries \(+2\), so cobalt must be \(+3\).

Ligands are named in ALPHABETICAL order regardless of charge, so aqua comes first, then cyanido, then ethane-1,2-diamine. That last name already contains a multiplying prefix, so it takes BIS rather than "di" and is enclosed in brackets:
AQUACYANIDOBIS(ETHANE-1,2-DIAMINE)COBALT(III) ION

In alphabetical ordering the prefixes themselves are ignored — it is the ligand name that counts, which is why "ethane-1,2-diamine" is placed by its own initial letter and not by "bis".

(b) The six ammine ligands are neutral and two chlorides sit outside, so nickel is \(+2\). The complex is the CATION, so it takes no \(-\mathrm{ate}\) suffix, and the counter ion is named last as a separate word:
HEXAAMMINENICKEL(II) CHLORIDE

Note the double "m" in ammine, which distinguishes the ligand ammonia from an organic amine.
